Migrating from Rust to SLA: Rewrite Checklist and Scenario Guide

This page gathers the conclusions of the previous pages into two executable things: a “Rust spelling → SLA rewrite” comparison checklist, and a decision table for “which to use in which scenario”. All numbers note their source document, version number, and date framing; they are assessment snapshots from a particular point in time, not permanent guarantees.

Three Judgments Before You Start

  1. Surface compatibility ≠ semantic compatibility. SLA's goal is to let a large amount of Rust code parse as-is and silently absorb redundant declarations during lowering, but the semantic layer is always different (reversed mutability, &self currently covers read and write, no proc-macro). The comparison documents explicitly list this as a common misunderstanding: “SLA is compatible with Rust syntax” refers only to the surface (Phase 1 about 70%).
  2. Runtime performance is not a selling point. Measured on 2026-10-22: Rust release's native/WASM runtime medians are about 1.47×/1.44× faster respectively (excluding the matmul outlier), Rust is faster for cold compilation of conventional source code; for hot compilation Rust is still faster on large source code, but the gap disappears or even reverses on small WASM projects; but with both sides in their size-optimal configurations, a typical SLA WASM load is about 1/5 the size of Rust's (matmul is an exception). Migration reasons should not be built on runtime or compilation speed, see the SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking) page for details.
  3. Maturity must be read with its date framing. For example, the no-fallback mainline convergence progress is recorded in roadmap_status_cn.md (v0.1 / 2026-07-01) as: No-fallback sweep 58/69 (84%), Y/shared-lowering 72%, Direct SAB fallback-removal 88%, weighted total progress about 80%. When citing it you must include this version and date; do not relay it as the current state.

Rewrite Checklist (Check Item by Item)

#Rust spellingSLA rewriteNotes
1let mut x = ...;let x = ...;Remove mut. let mut is never accepted; SLA's let is mutable by default
2&mut T / &mut self&T / &selfPhase 1 does not recognize &mut; mut must be removed manually; use Cell/RefCell for interior mutability
3'a / 'staticDelete directlyLifetimes are parsed only and do not enter semantics
4pub / pub(crate)Delete directlySA defaults to everything being linker-visible
5where T: BoundEither keep or deleteAfter parsing, bounds are used only for trait method lookup during monomorphization
6use std::foo::bar;@import "sa_std/foo/bar.sai"Both are accepted, but @import is the current spelling
7println!("…") / vec![…] / assert!(…)println("…") and other function calls without !The compatibility path recommends that the parser fault-tolerantly strip a ! immediately adjacent to an identifier, but source code should be written directly in function form
8panic!("string")panic(numeric code)When text is needed, go through sa_std's panic_msg
9impl Drop for XExpand the cleanup order by handThe Drop trait is not supported; release is implicitly injected by the compiler
10#[derive(X)] / #[inline]@derive / inline@derive is a compiler built-in whitelist system (the comparison documents record 6 of them, in the Phase 2 scope); do not assume an arbitrary derive is usable
11unsafe { … }Wrap the whole function in @ffi_wrapperBlock-level unsafe counts only as a “declaration of intent”; raw-pointer descent must be inside function-level isolation
12extern "C" fn@extern fnDual track
13#[test]@test "name"() { … }Landed
14loop { … break … }, range forwhile loops + break/continueThis is how 22_break_continue and 23_nested_loops in rosetta were changed
15Trait generic dispatch, dyn polymorphismMonomorphized static dispatch + vtable macro pathNo trait coherence, no GAT
16Complex expansion of proc-macro / macro_rules!macro hygienic macros or ordinary helper functionsMulti-arm pattern macros, fragment types, etc. are explicitly not introduced
17Async runtimes such as tokio::…async/.await/future<T> are usable, but there is no tokio equivalentServer-side code depending on a runtime ecosystem is not suitable to migrate for now
18Crates such as serde / regex / database driversBuilt-in JSON, regular expressions to be added via plugins, DB via plugins, or bc2sa bridgingSee the Standard Library, Error Handling, and async Compared page

Paired Examples: Four High-Frequency Rewrite Types

① Remove mut; Hand Interior Mutability to Cell

// Rust（demos/rosetta/59_method_counter/main.rs）
struct Counter(i32);

impl Counter {
    fn inc(&mut self) {
        self.0 += 1;
    }
}

// Sla（同目录 main.sla，节选）
struct Counter {
    value: Cell<i32>,
}

impl Counter {
    fn inc(&self) -> void {
        let current = self.value.get();
        self.value.set(current + 1);
    }
}

Note that the method signature is &self rather than &mut self: SLA's current &self covers both read and write uses, backed by the Referee.

② Expand a Drop Guard into an Explicit Sequence

// Rust（101_custom_drop，节选）
impl Drop for Guard<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.tally.set(self.tally.get() + self.value);
    }
}

// Sla（同目录 main.sla，节选）：按作用域顺序手工累加
tally = tally + inner_value;
tally = tally + outer_value;
return tally + result;

③ Adjust the Control-Flow Shape: loop/break/continue → while

// Rust（22_break_continue，节选）
loop {
    i += 1;
    if i % 2 == 0 { continue; }
    if i > 5 { break; }
    sum += i;
}

// Sla（同目录 main.sla，节选）
while 1 == 1 {
    i = i + 1;
    if i % 2 == 0 { continue; };
    if i > 5 { break; };
    sum = sum + i;
};

Compound assignment (+= etc.) is listed as a synonym mapping item on the compatibility path and desugars to x = x op y; while the current rosetta spelling generally writes it directly as x = x + y, and it is recommended to do the same when migrating, to avoid one layer of the compatibility surface.

④ Entry Signature and Self-Check Block

Rust's fn main() is usually written in SLA as returning i32 with an explicit return 0;, plus an @test block to lock in the observable result:

// Rust                          // Sla
fn main() {                      fn main() -> i32 {
    let msg = Message::Move          let msg = Message::Move { x: 10, y: 20 };
        { x: 10, y: 20 };            let result = process_msg(msg);
    println!("{}",                   println("{}", result);
        process_msg(msg));           return 0;
}                                }

@test "rosetta 006 enum and match"() {
    let result = process_msg(Message::Move { x: 10, y: 20 });
    if result != 30 { panic(6); };
}
NoteAfter migrating, run sla check first, then sla test; that is how the @test blocks in the rosetta tree are used. But do not forget that not everything in that tree passes end to end, so verify each one before bringing it into your own project.

Scenario Selection: When to Use What

Use Rust (Migrating to SLA Is Not Recommended)

  • Heavy-ecosystem scenarios such as desktop applications and server backends
  • Need a production-grade async runtime such as tokio / actix / axum
  • Need the full capability of serde, or large frameworks such as bevy / wgpu / iced
  • Many Rust veterans on the team, need for a mature IDE experience, large multi-person collaboration projects

Use SLA (No Need to Go to Rust)

  • WASM edge computing (Cloudflare Workers / Vercel Edge and the like) and WASM games / browser interaction
  • Embedded WASM / IoT displays (with both sides in their size-optimal configurations, typical size is about 1/5 of Rust's, but matmul is an exception and runtime is slower, so check against the load)
  • LLM sandboxes / Agent execution environments (error messages are simple and structured; the self-repair loop is native)
  • Domains needing verifier provability, such as safety / aviation
  • Teaching, educational ECS / game jams (simple syntax, low onboarding cost; compilation speed is not an advantage)

Use bc2sa Bridging (the Unique Path)

  • Have an existing Rust crate you do not want to rewrite, but need to deploy to the WASM edge
  • Want to use a C/C++ math library and also want SA verification
  • Want to consume serde / image / algorithm libraries, while accepting the current output size and compilation time
Warningbc2sa can currently only consume the O0 baseline plus the integer-operations subset (about 30% of real code, 2026-06-15 assessment framing); before submitting you must force -Copt-level=0 or first do opt --reg2mem. See the coverage and gap table on the The rosetta Comparison Set and the bc2sa Bridge Ecosystem page for details.

Decision Quick Reference

ScenarioRecommendation
WASM games / Bevy-style ECS (sa3d)SLA
SAX UI component handlers, LLM Agents writing code, third-party business packagesSLA
Edge Worker deploymentSLA
Need to use Rust serde / image / algorithm libraries, C/C++ math libraries, or a Rust crate but deploy to WASMbc2sa bridging + SLA calls
Heavy Web backends (axum), desktop GUIs (iced), OS / driversRust
Internal plugin developmentZig + SA (unchanged)

rust_vs_sla_final_cn.md §5 once gave a 16-dimension score (v0.2 / 2026-06-15; the “total score” row is the total as summarized by that document itself, which may differ slightly from adding the items, so cite the original text as authoritative):

The same document also records the v0.1 → v0.2 correction trajectory: ecosystem raised from 10 to 45 (the bc2sa entry was added), async from 60 to 80, toolchain from 30 to 50, and the total from 940 to 1085–1135. The value of this set of numbers is to show that the advantageous dimensions are completely different, not to claim which is stronger.

For engineering-side maturity, follow the roadmap (roadmap_status_cn.md v0.1 / 2026-07-01): No-fallback sweep 58/69, Y/shared-lowering 72%, Direct SAB fallback-removal 88%, weighted total progress about 80%; the remaining 11 failing tests are distributed across calls/assignments (Phase 3), std metadata (Phase 4), aggregates/enums/Derive (Phase 5), protocol iterators (Phase 6), and async (Phase 8). For later versions, check that document again for the latest numbers.

Final Checklist

  1. Search the whole text for mut: delete let mut and &mut, and replace interior mutability with Cell/RefCell
  2. Delete all lifetime annotations and pub modifiers
  3. Replace all use … with @import "…"; remove all ! suffixes from macro calls
  4. Change panic!("…") to panic(numeric code)
  5. Expand impl Drop into explicit cleanup statements and check the release order
  6. Wrap raw-pointer code in @ffi_wrapper functions
  7. Add an @test self-check block to each entry point; run sla check first, then sla test
  8. For parts depending on tokio / serde / large frameworks: confirm whether they stay on the Rust side, or switch to bc2sa bridging
  9. Manually check the changes against the rosetta demo on the same topic for semantic equivalence
